abstract: We present a framework for transfer learning based on modular variational Gaussian processes (GP). We develop a module-based method that having a dictionary of well fitted GPs, each model being characterised by its hyperparameters, pseudo-inputs and their corresponding posterior densities, one could build ensemble GP models without revisiting any data. Our method avoids undesired data centralisation, reduces rising computational costs and allows the transfer of learned uncertainty metrics after training. We exploit the augmentation of high-dimensional integral operators based on the Kullback-Leibler divergence between stochastic processes to introduce an efficient lower bound under all the sparse variational GPs, with different complexity and even likelihood distribution. The method is also valid for multi-output GPs, learning correlations a posteriori between independent modules. Extensive results illustrate the usability of our framework in large-scale and multi-task experiments, also compared with the exact inference methods in the literature.

summary.idea: The framework treats fitted Gaussian processes as reusable modules containing parameters, pseudo-inputs, and posterior distributions. A variational objective combines them into ensembles while transferring their learned uncertainty information.
summary.limitations: The approach assumes a dictionary of well-fitted component models. The abstract does not quantify approximation errors or establish that avoiding data centralization itself provides a formal privacy guarantee.
summary.problem: Combining knowledge from separately trained Gaussian processes can require collecting their original datasets again. That adds computation and can conflict with keeping data decentralized.
summary.results: Experiments illustrate large-scale and multitask use, including comparison with exact inference methods. The framework also handles differing likelihoods and can learn correlations between previously independent output modules.
summary.tldr: Reuse trained Gaussian-process modules and their uncertainty estimates without revisiting the original training data.

title: Modular Gaussian Processes for Transfer Learning

abstract: Large transformers are powerful architectures used for self-supervised data analysis across various data types, including protein sequences, images, and text. In these models, the semantic structure of the dataset emerges from a sequence of transformations between one representation and the next. We characterize the geometric and statistical properties of these representations and how they change as we move through the layers.By analyzing the intrinsic dimension (ID) and neighbor composition, we find that the representations evolve similarly in transformers trained on protein language taskand image reconstruction tasks. In the first layers, the data manifold expands, becoming high-dimensional, and then contracts significantly in the intermediate layers. In the last part of the model, the ID remains approximately constant or forms a second shallow peak. We show that the semantic information of the dataset is better expressed at the end of the first peak, and this phenomenon can be observed across many models trained on diverse datasets.Based on our findings, we point out an explicit strategy to identify, without supervision, the layers that maximize semantic content: representations at intermediate layers corresponding to a relative minimum of the ID profile are more suitable for downstream learning tasks.

summary.idea: The study tracks intrinsic dimension and neighborhood composition across layers. These geometric measurements describe how representations expand, compress, and organize examples during processing.
summary.limitations: The abstract reports recurring empirical patterns rather than a universal theorem for all transformers. It does not quantify downstream improvements or fully specify when the proposed layer-selection rule fails.
summary.problem: Transformer layers produce many possible representations, but the final layer may not be the most useful for a downstream task. Researchers need a way to identify informative layers without labels.
summary.results: Across the studied protein and image models, dimensions rise early and contract in intermediate layers. The authors propose choosing intermediate representations near a relative dimension minimum to capture useful semantic information.
summary.tldr: Use representation geometry to locate intermediate transformer layers that may be especially useful for downstream learning.

title: The geometry of hidden representations of large transformer models
